title: Acts 27:27–44
context: On the fourteenth night the sailors sense land and try to escape in the lifeboat, but Paul tells the centurion that unless they stay in the ship, the others cannot be saved, and the soldiers cut the boat loose. At dawn Paul urges everyone to eat, gives thanks to God before them all, and they are encouraged. The ship runs aground and breaks apart; the soldiers plan to kill the prisoners, but the centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them. Some swim and others float on planks, and all 276 reach land safely.

verses.text: But when the fourteenth night had come, as we were driven back and forth in the Adriatic Sea, about midnight the sailors surmised that they were drawing near to some land.
verses.arminianNotes: On the fourteenth night, drifting across the Adriatic Sea, as the term then covered the central Mediterranean, the sailors sense land is near.
verses.reformedNotes: Two weeks of drifting carried them some 475 miles from Cauda to Malta, a distance modern sailors have found consistent with the storm.

verses.text: They took soundings and found twenty fathoms. After a little while, they took soundings again, and found fifteen fathoms.
verses.arminianNotes: Their soundings show twenty fathoms, then fifteen. The bottom is rising fast.
verses.reformedNotes: The precise depths are another mark of an eyewitness account.

verses.text: Fearing that we would run aground on rocky ground, they let go four anchors from the stern, and wished for daylight.
verses.arminianNotes: Fearing rocks, they drop four anchors from the stern and pray for day.
verses.reformedNotes: Anchoring from the stern kept the bow toward shore, ready to run aground at dawn.

verses.text: As the sailors were trying to flee out of the ship and had lowered the boat into the sea, pretending that they would lay out anchors from the bow,
verses.arminianNotes: The sailors try to escape in the ship’s boat, pretending to lay out anchors from the bow.
verses.reformedNotes: Those with the skills to beach the ship try to save themselves and abandon everyone else.

verses.text: Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, “Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.”
verses.arminianNotes: Paul tells the centurion and soldiers, “Unless these stay in the ship, you can’t be saved.” Arminian theologians point to this verse to show that God’s promise of verse 24 was fulfilled through, and in some sense conditioned on, human cooperation; the outcome depended on what people did.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed theologians see a classic case of God ordaining both the end and the means. The lives were promised with certainty, yet the promise would be kept precisely by the sailors staying aboard, so Paul’s warning is itself one of the means God uses.

verses.text: Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the boat and let it fall off.
verses.arminianNotes: The soldiers cut the ropes of the boat and let it fall away. They act decisively on Paul’s word.
verses.reformedNotes: The pagan soldiers’ obedience to the prisoner’s warning becomes part of how God keeps his promise.

verses.text: While the day was coming on, Paul begged them all to take some food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day that you wait and continue fasting, having taken nothing.
verses.arminianNotes: As day is about to dawn, Paul urges everyone to eat, since they have gone fourteen days in suspense without food.
verses.reformedNotes: Paul cares for practical needs while waiting on God’s promise. Faith does not neglect the body.

verses.text: Therefore I beg you to take some food, for this is for your safety; for not a hair will perish from any of your heads.”
verses.arminianNotes: He urges them to eat for their survival, for not a hair will perish from anyone’s head, a phrase Jesus used in Luke 21:18.
verses.reformedNotes: The promise of safety does not make food unnecessary. Paul joins God’s assurance with ordinary means.

verses.text: When he had said this and had taken bread, he gave thanks to God in the presence of all; then he broke it and began to eat.
verses.arminianNotes: He takes bread, gives thanks to God in front of them all, breaks it, and begins to eat.
verses.reformedNotes: The words take, give thanks, and break recall the Last Supper and the feeding miracles, though this is a meal among mostly pagan sailors. Luke lets the echo stand without making it a sacrament.

verses.text: Then they all cheered up, and they also took food.
verses.arminianNotes: Everyone is encouraged and they eat too.
verses.reformedNotes: One man’s calm trust in God steadies a whole ship.

verses.text: In all, we were two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship.
verses.reformedNotes: Luke counts everyone because everyone will be saved. The number makes the fulfillment checkable.

verses.text: When they had eaten enough, they lightened the ship, throwing out the wheat into the sea.
verses.arminianNotes: When they have eaten, they lighten the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
verses.reformedNotes: The last of the cargo goes overboard so the ship can ride higher and run farther onto the beach.

verses.text: When it was day, they didn’t recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, and they decided to try to drive the ship onto it.
verses.arminianNotes: At daylight they do not recognize the land but see a bay with a beach and decide to run the ship ashore if they can.
verses.reformedNotes: Traditionally identified as St. Paul’s Bay on Malta.

verses.text: Casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time untying the rudder ropes. Hoisting up the foresail to the wind, they made for the beach.
verses.arminianNotes: They cut the anchors, loosen the rudder ropes, hoist the foresail, and make for the beach.
verses.reformedNotes: Every maneuver is careful seamanship. God’s promise does not make skill unnecessary.

verses.text: But coming to a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground. The bow struck and remained immovable, but the stern began to break up by the violence of the waves.
verses.arminianNotes: They strike a sandbar where two currents meet; the bow sticks fast and the stern is broken apart by the surf.
verses.reformedNotes: The wreck comes exactly as Paul foretold in verse 26.

verses.text: The soldiers’ counsel was to kill the prisoners, so that none of them would swim out and escape.
verses.arminianNotes: The soldiers plan to kill the prisoners so none can swim away and escape.
verses.reformedNotes: Roman guards could be executed for losing prisoners. Their plan is cruel but grimly logical.

verses.text: But the centurion, desiring to save Paul, stopped them from their purpose, and commanded that those who could swim should throw themselves overboard first to go toward the land;
verses.arminianNotes: The centurion, wanting to save Paul, stops them and orders those who can swim to jump first and make for land.
verses.reformedNotes: Julius’s regard for Paul spares every prisoner. God’s grant of all lives in verse 24 is kept through a soldier’s decision.

verses.text: and the rest should follow, some on planks and some on other things from the ship. So they all escaped safely to the land.
verses.arminianNotes: The rest follow on planks or pieces of the ship, and so all are brought safely to land.
verses.reformedNotes: The chapter ends on the fulfillment of the promise: all 276 reach shore, as God said.
